claim: Relative to an unmodified LLM, LLM policy violations can be reduce by 50% or more by augmenting the LLM with an additional attention head that reweights tokens likely to induce policy violation.
subclaims: Compared to what baseline are LLM policy violations reduced?
By how much can LLM policy violations be reduced?
What is added to the LLM to reduce policy violations?
What does the additional attention head do?
baseline_experiments: To address subclaim 1, compare the proposed augmented model against a clearly defined unmodified baseline of the same base LLM, using identical decoding settings, prompts, and evaluation criteria. Use a public safety-relevant prompt set such as HarmBench, AdvBench, or Anthropic/hh-rlhf harmlessness data from HuggingFace. First measure the policy-violation rate of the unmodified LLM using an automated safety classifier plus a smaller human-audited subset. Then measure the same rate after adding the proposed attention-head intervention, without changing system prompts, refusal templates, RLHF weights, or decoding parameters. If the augmented model shows a substantially lower violation rate while preserving general helpfulness on a public utility benchmark such as MT-Bench or AlpacaEval, this would support the claim that the relevant baseline is an unmodified LLM and that the reduction is attributable to the added mechanism. If improvements disappear when prompts, decoding, or classifiers are controlled, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary if the claimant provided full baseline model identity, decoding settings, prompt set, raw generations, and violation labels for both baseline and augmented models.

To address subclaim 2, estimate whether policy violations can be reduced by 50% or more using a statistically powered evaluation on public datasets. Use held-out harmful-instruction prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, and a jailbreak-oriented dataset such as JailbreakBench, ensuring none were used to train the token-reweighting mechanism. Evaluate violation rates for the unmodified LLM and the augmented LLM, then compute relative reduction: (baseline violation rate - augmented violation rate) / baseline violation rate. Use bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar's test on paired prompt outcomes. If the lower bound of the confidence interval exceeds 50% across at least one broad benchmark, and ideally across multiple benchmarks, the quantitative claim is supported. If the point estimate is below 50%, or the confidence interval overlaps much smaller reductions, the claim is not established. If the reduction is large only on one narrow dataset, the claim may be feasible but not generally demonstrated. This experiment could be made unnecessary by credible third-party benchmark results with paired prompt-level outcomes and confidence intervals showing at least a 50% relative reduction.

To address subclaims 3 and 4, perform an ablation and mechanistic validation of the added attention head that is claimed to reweight tokens likely to induce policy violation. Implement the added head so its attention weights or token-level scores are inspectable, and train or calibrate it using a public dataset with harmful versus benign prompts, such as HarmBench plus benign instruction data from OpenAssistant or Alpaca. Evaluate four variants on held-out public safety prompts: the unmodified LLM, the LLM with the added head active, the LLM with the added head randomly initialized or shuffled, and the LLM with the head present but its reweighting disabled. Also measure whether tokens receiving high reweighting scores correspond to harmful trigger tokens or phrases by comparing them with token-level rationales generated by human annotators or a separate classifier, and test whether suppressing or masking those high-scoring tokens reduces violations. If only the active learned head reduces violations and its weights concentrate on policy-relevant tokens, this supports the mechanism that the added attention head performs meaningful reweighting of violation-inducing tokens. If random or disabled variants perform similarly, or if the head attends mostly to irrelevant tokens, the proposed mechanism is not supported even if overall safety improves. This experiment could be made unnecessary if the claimant released the trained head, architecture details, ablation results, and token-level attribution analyses showing that the head specifically identifies and reweights policy-risk tokens.
method_experiments: To address subclaim 1 ('Compared to what baseline are LLM policy violations reduced?') and subclaim 2 ('By how much can LLM policy violations be reduced?'), run a controlled before/after evaluation on the same open-weight instruction model, e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct or Mistral-7B-Instruct, comparing the unmodified model against the augmented model on public safety datasets such as HarmBench, SALAD-Bench/SALAD-Base-Test, ToxicChat, and RealToxicityPrompts. Use identical prompts, decoding settings, system prompts, and refusal policies for both models. Score outputs with at least two evaluators: an automated safety judge such as LlamaGuard or MD-Judge, plus a toxicity/safety classifier such as a Jigsaw-finetuned toxicity model; optionally add a small human audit sample. Primary metric: policy violation rate or attack success rate. Test whether the augmented model reduces violations by at least 50%, e.g. from 20% to 10% or lower, with bootstrap confidence intervals across prompts and stratified results by harm category. If the reduction is >=50% with overlapping evaluator agreement and no large degradation in benign helpfulness, this supports the main claim. If reduction is smaller, inconsistent across datasets, or only appears under one judge, the claim is weakened. If the unmodified baseline is not clearly specified or is already safety-tuned to near-zero violation rate, the 50% claim may be ill-posed. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary if the proponents provide full paired prompt-level outputs, scoring code, baseline definition, and confidence intervals on public benchmarks.

To address subclaim 3 ('What is added to the LLM to reduce policy violations?') and subclaim 4 ('What does the additional attention head do?'), perform an architectural ablation study comparing: (a) the unmodified model, (b) the model with the proposed additional attention head that reweights violation-inducing tokens, (c) the same number of added parameters but randomly initialized/frozen or trained without token-risk supervision, and (d) a simpler non-attention intervention such as logit biasing or a classifier-gated refusal layer. Train any needed token-risk supervision using public safety corpora such as SALAD-Base, HarmBench behaviors, ToxicChat, and RealToxicityPrompts, labeling tokens/spans associated with unsafe requests or unsafe completions. Evaluate on held-out datasets not used for training, such as SALAD-Attack-Enhanced-Subset and HarmBench. Measure both violation rate and whether the added head assigns higher weights or suppression scores to tokens/spans judged risky by an independent classifier or human annotation. If only condition (b) achieves large safety gains and its learned attention/reweighting aligns with risky tokens, this supports the claim that the added attention head and its token reweighting mechanism are responsible. If condition (c) or (d) performs similarly, the benefit may come from extra parameters, fine-tuning, refusal calibration, or classifier gating rather than the proposed head. If attention weights do not correlate with risky tokens, the claimed mechanism is undermined even if safety improves. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released model code, trained weights, token-level risk labels, and ablation results isolating the added head.

To address subclaim 2 ('By how much can LLM policy violations be reduced?') under realistic adversarial pressure, run an adaptive jailbreak robustness evaluation where public attack sets from HarmBench and SALAD-Attack-Enhanced-Subset are supplemented with automated paraphrase and jailbreak generation using an open model such as Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct or Llama-3-70B-Instruct. Keep the target model fixed and compare the unmodified and augmented versions across single-turn harmful requests, multi-turn escalation, role-play, encoding/obfuscation, and prompt-injection-style attacks. Use attack success rate, unsafe score, and severity-weighted harm as metrics, with the same safety judges as in the first experiment. Also measure benign refusal rate on harmless prompts from datasets such as AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, or a benign slice of ToxicChat to detect over-refusal. If the augmented model maintains a >=50% lower attack success rate across both static and adaptive attacks without a major increase in false refusals, the feasibility claim is strengthened. If the reduction disappears under adaptive attacks or comes mainly from refusing benign requests, the practical claim is weakened. Earlier benchmark results should inform which attack categories to emphasize here. This experiment could be made unnecessary if independent red-team evaluations already show prompt-level adaptive attack results, benign false-refusal rates, and severity-weighted safety outcomes for the exact augmented architecture.
